text: The Taliban has released a biography reaffirming Mullah Mohammed Omar as its leader, aiming to quash persistent rumors of his death and assert his continued authority amid rising competition from ISIS. The document details Omar’s early life, militant career against Soviet forces, and current role directing Taliban operations from hiding, despite no verified sightings or recordings in over a decade.

Hundreds gathered in Summerville, South Carolina, for the funeral of Walter Scott, a Black man fatally shot in the back by a white police officer during a traffic stop, an act mourners and clergy condemned as racially motivated. Officer Michael Slager was swiftly charged with murder after a bystander’s video contradicted his account, though a witness reported a prior scuffle, potentially complicating the case. Scott’s family and supporters vowed his death would spur national change, calling it both a racial and human rights issue.

A former TSA agent, Daniel Boykin, 33, was sentenced to six months in jail and 5.5 years of probation for secretly recording a female co-worker in a TSA-only restroom and burglarizing her home to obtain over 90 videos and 1,500 photos. Boykin pleaded guilty to unlawful photography, aggravated burglary, and computer crimes; the TSA confirmed he held an administrative role and was fired when the investigation began.

Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage—home to genres like morna and funana—as a key driver for economic growth, lacking traditional natural resources. Initiatives like the Kriol Jazz Festival and Atlantic Music Expo aim to boost tourism and global exposure, with music seen as central to the nation’s creative economy and international branding.

Arsenal kept title hopes alive with a 1-0 win at Burnley, moving within four points of leaders Chelsea ahead of their crucial clash next week. Meanwhile, Aston Villa and Leicester earned vital wins in the relegation battle, while Sunderland suffered a heavy defeat to Crystal Palace.

Original "Twin Peaks" cast members launched a #SaveTwinPeaks campaign supporting David Lynch amid his salary dispute with Showtime, calling a revival without him "like pies without cherries." Lynch exited the nine-episode reboot over insufficient funding to realize his vision, though Showtime says it still hopes to bring him back alongside co-creator Mark Frost.

Andrew Getty, 47, heir to the Getty oil fortune, died of apparent natural causes at his Los Angeles home; authorities found no signs of foul play. He had known health issues, including a serious medical condition diagnosed in 2013, and an autopsy is pending.

Maryland police say Nyia Parler, 41, cannot be extradited to Philadelphia on charges of abandoning her quadriplegic son in the woods until she completes unspecified medical treatment. Her 21-year-old son, found after four days in Cobbs Creek Park suffering from dehydration, malnutrition, and exposure, is now hospitalized; Parler faces multiple assault and endangerment charges.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named asteroid 316201 "Malala" in honor of Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai, recognizing her advocacy for girls' education. The 4-kilometer-wide asteroid, discovered in 2010, orbits between Mars and Jupiter every 5.5 years. Mainzer cited the need to celebrate women—especially women of color—in science and society.

Gastrointestinal illness has sickened 95 passengers and five crew members aboard the Celebrity Infinity, prompting CDC investigation. The ship, which departed San Diego on March 29 and last docked in Puerto Vallarta on April 10, is implementing enhanced cleaning and testing measures. This marks the third such outbreak on the vessel, following incidents in 2006 and 2013.

The entire "Star Wars" saga dropped on digital HD, sparking fan frenzy. Mindy Kaling’s brother admitted to posing as Black to gain medical school admission, drawing criticism including from his sister. Burger King sponsored a wedding for a couple named Burger and King, while Michelle Obama danced with "So You Think You Can Dance" stars at the White House Easter Egg Roll.
The FBI charged Philadelphia woman Keonna Thomas, 30, with attempting to travel to Syria to join

HBO released a teaser for "True Detective" Season 2, premiering June 21, starring Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams, and Taylor Kitsch. The season follows three law enforcement officers and a criminal entangled in a conspiracy amid California’s industrial underworld.

Authorities charged Carlos Colina, 32, in connection with the discovery of human remains in Cambridge, Massachusetts, identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, whom Colina knew. Colina faces charges of assault and battery causing serious bodily injury and improper disposal of a body; additional charges may follow pending forensic analysis. Remains were found in a duffel bag and a nearby apartment building common area, close to police headquarters.

Eastern High School basketball star Trey Moses asked freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to prom in a heartfelt gesture that went viral. The act, supported by Ellie’s parents and praised by school staff, highlights the impact of the school’s Best Buddies program fostering inclusion. Moses, bound for Ball State, plans to study special education, while Ellie eagerly anticipates dress shopping for the big night.

NBC debuts "A.D. The Bible Continues," a sequel to the 2013 hit "The Bible," airing Sundays starting Easter. Other notable premieres include the final season of "Mad Men," FX's returning "Louie" and new comedy "The Comedians," NBC's thriller "American Odyssey," and Netflix's "Marvel's Daredevil."

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence faces backlash for signing a religious freedom law critics say enables anti-LGBT discrimination, but the move bolsters his standing with the GOP’s ultraconservative base ahead of the 2016 presidential race. The controversy reflects a broader Republican push in multiple states to advance similar legislation, reigniting a national culture war over LGBT rights despite growing public support for same-sex marriage.

Apple’s latest iOS update introduces diverse emojis with multiple skin tones, same-sex couples, and new national flags, sparking both praise and backlash. The inclusion of non-white Santa emojis and LGBTQ+ representations has drawn particular attention, while some groups, like redheads and Armenians, feel overlooked. The move reflects broader demographic shifts and growing demands for digital inclusivity.

Avril Lavigne reveals she was bedridden for five months with Lyme disease, which left her unable to breathe, talk, or move. The singer, now 80% recovered, says the illness was a wake-up call and is releasing a new single to support the 2015 Special Olympics.

New research by the Anne Frank House indicates Anne and Margot Frank likely died of typhus in Bergen-Belsen at least a month earlier than the previously accepted date of March 1945, based on survivor testimonies and archival records. The sisters, severely weakened and lice-infested, probably succumbed in February 1945 during a deadly typhus outbreak.

Two Troy University students, Ryan Calhoun and Delonte Martistee, were arrested and charged with gang rape during spring break in Panama City Beach, Florida. The Bay County Sheriff’s Office identified the victim from a video found in an unrelated investigation and confirmed the assault occurred between March 10–12, 2015; both students have been suspended, and Martistee removed from the track team. Authorities say more arrests are expected as the investigation continues.

A stray dog in Washington State survived being hit by a car, bludgeoned with a hammer, and buried alive, later staggering to a farm where she was rescued. Named Theia, the one-year-old bully mix suffered severe injuries but is recovering thanks to veterinary care and over $10,000 in public donations. Her story echoes that of a Florida cat recently found alive days after burial following a similar ordeal.

The FBI confirmed that Zulkifli bin Hir, aka Marwan—a top wanted terrorist and bomb maker linked to Jemaah Islamiyah—was killed in a January raid in the southern Philippines. The operation, which targeted Marwan in a Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters stronghold, resulted in 44 elite Philippine police commandos dead and jeopardized a fragile peace deal with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.

A framework nuclear deal with Iran allows it to retain key nuclear infrastructure and receive billions in sanctions relief, despite concerns it could still pursue weapons. Critics argue the agreement lacks robust inspection mechanisms and long-term constraints, warning it repeats past failures like the 1994 North Korea accord. Meanwhile, Iran continues supporting militant groups across the Middle East even as negotiations advance.

"Mad Men" returns for its final episodes amid the cultural upheaval of late 1969, as its characters navigate personal and professional disintegration against a backdrop of societal change. The series, which has mirrored the decade’s unraveling ideals, is expected to conclude with Don Draper alone and adrift, symbolizing the end of an era.

Katie, a giraffe at the Dallas Zoo, gave birth live on Animal Planet’s stream to a roughly 6-foot-tall calf after an hour-long labor. The newborn showed positive signs—moving its ears, attempting to stand and nurse—with its gender still unknown. The event drew online viewers and onlookers from nearby giraffes, including Katie’s companion Jade.

President Obama’s historic nomination of Loretta Lynch as the first African-American woman attorney general faces an unprecedented Senate confirmation delay, now exceeding six months. Supporters allege racial bias and partisan obstruction, while Republicans cite policy disagreements and unrelated legislative disputes; Lynch cleared the Judiciary Committee in February but awaits a full Senate vote.

Three killed, five wounded in armed assault on Balkh province attorney general's office; Afghan forces engaged in ongoing firefight with assailants. Two police officers and a security guard among the dead; operations proceeding cautiously to avoid civilian casualties.

Bob Barker, 91, made a surprise return to "The Price Is Right" on April 1, hosting the first game before handing off to Drew Carey. The former longtime host, who retired in 2007, appeared sharp and energetic during his brief comeback.

Blues legend B.B. King, 89, was hospitalized for dehydration linked to Type II diabetes but has since been discharged and is resting at home. His daughter and publicist confirmed he is feeling much better and spending time with family. This marks a recurrence of health issues that forced tour cancellations last year.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing. The article argues that preventing future extremism requires addressing real Muslim grievances—not reforming Islam—and showing young Muslims that violence harms, rather than helps, their communities.

CNN highlights top videos of the week: a tour of Mike Tyson’s abandoned Ohio mansion, set to become a church; footage of the Fury 325 roller coaster; an exclusive interview with Bikram Choudhury accuser Sarah Baughn; a shepherd’s eyewitness account of the Germanwings crash; and a debate on Indiana’s religious freedom law featuring Penn Jillette.
Coalition forces have reclaimed 25–30% of Iraqi territory previously held by ISIS, with gains concentrated

A passenger on Air Canada Flight 8623 from Toronto to Atlanta attempted to choke soccer player Oliver Minatel with a cord during descent, prompting intervention by fellow passengers. The suspect, who claimed the team was trying to kill him, was not restrained but kept seated until landing, when he was taken into custody and sent for mental evaluation. No federal charges are pending, but the case is under review by the U.S. Attorney’s Office.

Briton Rurik Jutting, a former banker, is charged with murdering two Indonesian women—Sumarti Ningsih and Seneng Mujiasih—in his Hong Kong apartment in November. The case was adjourned until May to analyze over 200 pieces of forensic evidence; both victims, domestic workers, were found dead in the upmarket Wan Chai residence.

A massive tornado tore through northern Illinois, killing one person in Fairdale and destroying or damaging dozens of homes, including the sheriff’s residence, though widespread fatalities were averted thanks to early warnings. The storm cut a 22-mile path through Ogle County, flattening structures like the local Grubsteakers restaurant, while multiple other tornadoes struck the Midwest over two days.

Don McLean’s original manuscript for “American Pie” sold for $1.2 million at Christie’s, marking the third-highest price for an American literary manuscript. The 16-page draft, containing lyrics and notes, was auctioned as McLean, nearing 70, sought to secure his family’s future. The song, inspired by Buddy Holly’s death and long subject to interpretation, topped charts in 1972 despite its 8-minute length.

UNRWA chief Pierre Krähenbühl to make emergency visit to Syria’s Yarmouk refugee camp amid deepening humanitarian crisis, with 18,000 civilians—including 3,500 children—trapped under armed group control and cut off from aid since late 2013. The camp, once home to 160,000, has been devastated by fighting between Syrian

Intense Saudi-led airstrikes and ground fighting in Yemen have killed an estimated 600 people in under two weeks, devastated infrastructure, and left 16 million without electricity as the Houthis retain control of Sanaa. The ICRC urgently appeals for a humanitarian ceasefire to deliver medical aid, while the UN Security Council remains deadlocked over a Russian-drafted resolution calling for a halt to bombing. Meanwhile, al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula exploits the chaos, expanding its influence amid the collapse of central authority.

Legendary Australian cricketer and broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at age 84 after battling skin cancer. Revered as both a record-breaking player—Australia’s first to achieve 2,000 Test runs and 200 wickets—and cricket’s most iconic commentator, Benaud was mourned globally, with tributes from figures including Australian PM Tony Abbott and British PM David Cameron.

A brief total lunar eclipse—lasting just 4 minutes 43 seconds, the shortest of the century—occurred early morning over western North America, visible partially across the U.S. and in parts of South America, Asia, and Russia. The event is the third in a rare tetrad of total lunar eclipses, with the next due September 28.

Federal prosecutors have charged Robert Durst, 71, with unlawful firearm possession after a .38 caliber revolver was found in his New Orleans hotel room; he is already held without bail on a first-degree murder charge in the 2000 killing of Susan Berman and faces possible extradition to Los Angeles, where conviction could bring the death penalty. Authorities also seized drugs, cash, a latex mask, and a UPS package containing over $100,000, while FBI agents review decades-old cold cases linked to Durst’s past residences. His attorney cites serious health issues, including recent brain and esophageal surgeries, and claims authorities are grasping at straws.

Paul Walker's death in 2013 during a break from filming "Furious 7" deeply affected fans and co-stars, prompting an outpouring of tributes. The film was completed using CGI and his brothers as stand-ins, culminating in a poignant farewell to his character. At the premiere, Vin Diesel called it "more than a movie," reflecting widespread grief and admiration for Walker’s kindness and legacy.

On Thursday’s “The Price Is Right,” model Manuela Arbelaez accidentally revealed the correct price for a Hyundai Sonata, gifting contestant a car; host Drew Carey laughed off the blunder. The slip-up followed former host Bob Barker’s surprise appearance the day before.

Thai Smile Airways unveiled an Airbus A320 wrapped in "Adventure Time" livery featuring Finn, Jake, and Princess Bubblegum, with themed interiors including seat headrests and airsickness bags. The special aircraft results from a partnership with Cartoon Network Amazone water park near Pattaya, ahead of its inaugural Bangkok-to-Phuket flight on April 4.

A mother duck and her brood caused a commotion on a busy Washington, D.C., street Tuesday, prompting pedestrians to halt traffic and guide them to safety. Onlookers used an umbrella to corral the ducklings and escorted the family to a nearby grassy area, drawing coverage from national news outlets.

French investigators have completed evidence collection at the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site in the Alps, with only private security remaining. The co-pilot, Andreas Lubitz, is believed to have deliberately crashed the plane, killing all 150 on board; both black boxes were recovered and initial data confirms intentional descent. Authorities have identified 150 DNA profiles and 470 personal items, including damaged phones unlikely to yield data.

Cuba attends the Summit of the Americas for the first time since 1962 after the U.S. dropped its opposition, amid ongoing talks to restore diplomatic ties and reopen embassies. Tensions flared in Panama as pro- and anti-Castro groups clashed, while Cuba insists full normalization hinges on its removal from the U.S. terrorism sponsor list—a move the State Department has recommended. Despite warming U.S.-Cuba relations, Havana continues to strongly back Venezuela, a key ally, even as Washington downplays Caracas as a security threat.

Jesus and his disciples relied on financial support from followers, particularly women like Mary Magdalene and Joanna, who provided resources from their own means. Wealthy patrons such as Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus also contributed, enabling the ministry to function at a subsistence level through donations, hospitality, and shared provisions.

The California Public Utilities Commission ordered PG&E to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe gas pipeline operations, including the 2010 San Bruno explosion that killed eight and destroyed 37 homes. Most of the penalty—$850 million—will fund pipeline safety upgrades, with PG&E pledging to become the nation’s safest energy company.

Lauren Hill, 19, died after a public battle with terminal brain cancer, having inspired millions by fulfilling her dream of playing college basketball. Mount St. Joseph University moved its season opener to accommodate her, and she raised $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research before her death. Tributes poured in globally, hailing her courage, positivity, and legacy of perseverance.

A massive fire erupted Friday morning at General Electric’s Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, prompting a four-alarm response and blanketing the area in thick smoke. No injuries or trapped individuals were reported, and the cause remains under investigation.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, a key figure in nuclear talks with the U.S., is known for his diplomatic finesse and U.S. education but has a complex past, including involvement in revolutionary-era protests and disputed biographical details. Despite past controversies, he now works closely with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry to finalize a nuclear deal by the June 30 deadline.

A Connecticut juvenile court denied a motion to release 17-year-old Cassandra C., who is in remission after months of court-ordered chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma, from state custody. Her attorneys argue she’s no longer at imminent risk and should return home, but the state maintains she remains a flight risk until treatment ends later this month.

New research using psychological text analysis strongly suggests Shakespeare co-wrote "Double Falsehood" with John Fletcher, contradicting long-held doubts about its authenticity. The study found the play’s language closely matches Shakespeare’s in the first half and splits between him and Fletcher in the second, with minimal traces of later editor Lewis Theobald.

French prosecutor Brice Robin denied the existence of any onboard video from Germanwings Flight 9525, contradicting reports by Bild and Paris Match claiming a recovered cell phone video showed the crash’s final moments. Authorities and France’s BEA stated no such footage has been found or analyzed, while Lufthansa confirmed co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had a history of depression but held a valid medical certificate.

Emy Afalava, a U.S. veteran born in American Samoa—a U.S. territory since 1900—is denied citizenship and voting rights despite the Fourteenth Amendment’s birthright clause. He and other American Samoans are challenging this exclusion in a federal lawsuit before the D.C. Circuit, seeking to end the last remaining exception to birthright citizenship in U.S. territories.

Blue Bell Creameries has shut down its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, plant and issued a recall after listeria was found in a 3-ounce ice cream cup linked to a Kansas hospital outbreak. The CDC warns against consuming affected products marked with codes O–T, though the bacteria doesn’t match all patient samples; five hospitalized patients in Kansas fell ill, three fatally, after consuming Blue Bell milkshakes. This marks Blue Bell’s first recall in its 108-year history amid ongoing investigations into potential links to listeriosis cases.

Al-Shabaab claimed a deadly attack on Garissa University College in Kenya, taking hostages and killing many, marking an escalation in its cross-border campaign. The group, linked to al-Qaeda and rooted in Somalia’s civil conflict, exploits religious, ethnic, and governance failures to fuel recruitment and violence across East Africa.

The U.S. has lodged a formal complaint with Russia after a Russian SU-27 jet intercepted a U.S. RC-135U reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in what the Pentagon called an "unsafe and unprofessional" maneuver in international airspace. The U.S. denies Russian claims the American aircraft had its transponder off, calling the assertion false; this marks the latest in a series of tense aerial encounters between the two nations.

A hooded black-winged angel sculpture appeared near the site where Walter Scott was fatally shot by police in North Charleston, quickly becoming a symbol for Black Lives Matter protests. Created by local artist Phillip Hyman from reclaimed wood and black paint, the piece expresses mourning and has been carried daily to demonstrations at City Hall.

North Charleston police officer Michael Slager was fired and charged with murder after a bystander’s video showed him shooting unarmed Walter Scott five times as Scott fled. The footage contradicts Slager’s initial claim that Scott had taken his Taser, and witness Feidin Santana said he saw no such struggle. An ongoing investigation by South Carolina authorities is examining the incident.

Nashville’s district attorney banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals after public outcry, though similar offers—mostly to men—have occurred nationwide for years. While involuntary sterilization was historically tied to eugenics and deemed unconstitutional in some contexts, voluntary sterilization as part of a plea deal may be legally permissible, raising ethical questions about gender bias and punishment norms.

Over 25,000 Ebola cases and 10,000 deaths have occurred in the past year, with 30 new cases reported the week of April 5—the lowest weekly total since May 2014. While Liberia and Sierra Leone see declining demand for treatment beds, Guinea reports unsafe burials and post-mortem diagnoses, suggesting hidden transmission chains persist.

The NCAA, long claiming education is central to college athletics, now argues in court it has no legal duty to ensure academic integrity for student-athletes, despite its public commitments and eligibility rules. This stance comes amid a lawsuit over UNC’s 18-year academic fraud scandal, drawing criticism as contradictory and undermining the NCAA’s foundational principles.

Six injured in explosion and fire at a paraxylene (PX) chemical plant in Zhangzhou, Fujian province, following an oil leak; over 600 firefighters contained the blaze. The facility, relocated from Xiamen after 2007 protests over pollution fears, previously exploded in 2013 with no casualties reported.

A bystander’s video showing Officer Michael Slager shooting Walter Scott in the back as he fled has reignited calls for mandatory police body cameras to prevent such killings and restore public trust. The author argues that while body cameras are costly, they reduce use-of-force incidents and could help expose and counteract systemic racial bias in policing until deeper societal reforms take hold.

The VII Summit of the Americas in Panama City, centered on the historic U.S.-Cuba rapprochement and anticipated Obama-Castro handshake, has been overshadowed by rising tensions over Venezuela. President Maduro’s accusations of a U.S.-led coup plot and Washington’s sanctions on Venezuelan officials have drawn strong regional backlash, with Cuba publicly siding with Venezuela, creating a “triangle of tension” that threatens to dominate the summit.

A nuclear submarine under repair at Russia's Zvyozdochka shipyard caught fire during welding work, igniting rubber insulation between its hulls. Authorities confirmed the vessel had no nuclear fuel, weapons, or hazardous materials onboard, and no injuries were reported.

Tropical storm Maysak (Chedeng), downgraded from a super typhoon, neared the Philippines with sustained winds of 70 mph, prompting evacuations and bans on coastal activities. Authorities warned of flash floods and landslides as the storm headed for a Sunday landfall in Isabela province, with officials urging residents to prepare for severe impacts.

Deion Sanders publicly chided his son, Deion Jr., on Twitter for claiming to eat only "hood doughnuts," reminding him of his trust fund and affluent lifestyle. The SMU wide receiver and aspiring entrepreneur took the rebuke in stride, retweeting his father’s comments.

Adelma Cifuentes survived years of brutal domestic abuse in rural Guatemala, including an attempted femicide that cost her an arm, before securing justice with her husband sentenced to 27 years. Her case reflects a national crisis: Guatemala ranks third globally in femicides, with deep-rooted machismo, postwar impunity, and weak institutions fueling epidemic gender-based violence. Grassroots groups, legal reforms, and international efforts are slowly driving change, but most cases go unpunished and millions of women remain at risk.

Police in Malegaon, Maharashtra, are requiring residents to register their cattle with photos and unique identifiers to enforce a state-wide beef ban and combat cow slaughter. Over 100 owners have complied as authorities build a database to verify livestock amid heightened penalties, including five-year jail terms for beef-related offenses. The move has sparked backlash from traders and consumers, with similar strict laws emerging in other Indian states.

Lucknow police in northern India have acquired pepper-spraying drones for crowd control during violent protests, sparking debate over civil liberties and authoritarian tactics. Each drone, costing up to $19,300, carries a camera and pepper spray and follows broader drone use in India for surveillance, disaster relief, and law enforcement.

Don McLean's handwritten manuscript of "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's. The 1971 song, a cultural touchstone referencing the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly and others, remains one of America’s most iconic and enduring anthems.

A meticulously planned heist over Easter weekend saw thieves break into a London vault in Hatton Garden, echoing classic capers like the 1971 Baker Street robbery. Unlike cybercrime trends, the gang used old-school tactics, likely aided by inside information, targeting cash and easily liquidated valuables. Police are pursuing forensic leads, CCTV, and criminal networks, treating the case as a major but non-violent challenge.

7-Eleven launches its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day at U.S. stores Saturday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., offering $1.49 fills in any sanitary container that fits through a 10-inch hole—excluding garbage cans. The event kicks off peak Slurpee season and differs from the annual Free Slurpee Day on July 11.

Former Kentucky State Senator Georgia Davis Powers sharply criticized Rand Paul’s presidential campaign launch, calling his outreach to minority voters disingenuous and citing his opposition to civil rights protections, voting rights, and the Department of Education. She accused Paul of promoting policies that would roll back decades of progress and deemed him unfit for national leadership.

A Lamborghini crashed at Walt Disney World Speedway’s Exotic Driving Experience, killing 36-year-old passenger Gary Terry; driver Tavon Watson, 24, was hospitalized with minor injuries. Operator Petty Holdings expressed condolences following the incident Sunday.

Aaron Hernandez’s defense rested after less than a day of testimony in his murder trial for the 2013 killing of Odin Lloyd, following months of prosecution evidence largely based on circumstantial details. Key points include Hernandez allegedly lying to Patriots owner Robert Kraft about his alibi before the murder time was public, his fiancée’s disposal of a suspicious box, and disputed forensic evidence linking his shoes and a possible gun to the crime scene. The jury is expected to begin deliberations soon after closing arguments.

Chinese authorities have detained women's rights activist Wu Rongrong and four others for "creating disturbances" after they planned an International Women's Day protest against sexual harassment. Their detention—amid China’s anticipated adoption of an anti-domestic violence law and the 20th anniversary of the Beijing Women’s Conference—highlights a broader crackdown on independent activism, with activists facing restricted legal access, medical care, and heightened government suspicion of civil society groups.

Martin O'Malley challenged the notion of Hillary Clinton's "inevitability" as the Democratic presidential nominee, citing historical precedents like her 2008 loss to Barack Obama. While acknowledging Clinton's qualifications, O'Malley emphasized the need for a robust primary debate and hinted at his own potential candidacy despite polling in the low single digits.

Odin Lloyd’s family delivered emotional victim impact statements as Aaron Hernandez was sentenced to life without parole for Lloyd’s 2013 murder. Lloyd, 27, was remembered as a devoted family man, hard worker, and semi-pro football player. His mother, Ursula Ward, expressed grief but also forgiveness for those involved in his killing.

Ted Cruz, positioning himself as the leading GOP evangelical candidate, campaigned aggressively in Iowa, leveraging his faith-based appeal to connect with the state’s influential Christian conservative base. He aims to unite evangelicals, tea party supporters, and libertarians into a winning coalition, while other potential rivals like Huckabee and Santorum also eye the same bloc. With religious liberty and social issues driving engagement, Cruz’s team sees untapped potential in mobilizing evangelical turnout ahead of the 2016 caucuses.

Marvel and other studios unveiled new character reveals across multiple superhero projects, including Paul Bettany as Vision in "Avengers: Age of Ultron," Charlie Cox's official Daredevil suit, Ben Hardy as Angel in "X-Men: Apocalypse," and Jamie Bell's CGI-rendered Thing in the "Fantastic Four" reboot. The flurry of announcements underscores the ongoing surge in superhero media ahead of major 2015 releases.

Nearly 1,000 migrants were rescued Friday in the Mediterranean off Libya’s coast, amid a surge in crossings from Africa and the Middle East. Over 10,000 have reached Italy since January, with at least 480 deaths this year—up sharply from last year—due to dangerous smuggling conditions.
TV5Monde regained partial control of its broadcast and social media after a major cyberattack Wednesday that knocked out 11 channels, websites, and accounts, some def

David Lynch has withdrawn as director of the "Twin Peaks" revival, citing insufficient funding to realize his vision. Showtime expressed disappointment but hopes to still produce the nine-episode season with both Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost involved.

High-profile trials of Aaron Hernandez and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev near conclusion in Massachusetts, with juries set to deliberate. Rand Paul officially launches presidential bid, while Chicago holds a mayoral runoff between Rahm Emanuel and Chuy Garcia. Ferguson, Missouri, holds elections under heightened scrutiny following Michael Brown’s death, with increased minority representation on the ballot.

Tornadoes struck parts of Kansas and Missouri Wednesday night, with sightings near Goddard, Aetna, and Potosi, causing wind damage, flooding, and hail. Nighttime tornadoes pose heightened danger, and more severe storms are forecast across the Midwest and Mississippi River Valley Thursday.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without parole for the 2008 first-degree murder of ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander, after two juries deadlocked on the death penalty. The judge imposed the harshest available sentence following emotional victim impact statements and Arias’s expression of remorse.

A Delaware family fell seriously ill after staying at a luxury villa in the U.S. Virgin Islands, where the EPA detected methyl bromide—a highly toxic, indoor-prohibited pesticide—likely from a nearby fumigation. The EPA and DOJ are investigating potential regulatory violations, with Terminix, the pest control company involved, cooperating; the family’s unit was not directly treated but may have been contaminated.

A Columbia Journalism School review found Rolling Stone's UVA gang rape article was the result of institutional failures in reporting, editing, and fact-checking. While the University of Virginia cannot sue for defamation as a government entity, individual members of the Phi Kappa Psi fraternity may pursue legal action if they can prove the false statements specifically targeted them and caused tangible harm.

FBI agents and task force officers confronted suspected serial armed robber Kevone Charleston, 36, outside a Georgia CVS, leading to a shootout and crash that injured two agents and wounded Charleston. Authorities say he is linked to 32 commercial robberies since 2013; all involved are expected to recover.

A Menzies Aviation ramp agent fell asleep in the pressurized cargo hold of Alaska Airlines Flight 448, prompting an emergency return to Seattle after banging and cries for help were heard mid-flight. The plane landed safely after 14 minutes airborne; the worker, unharmed and cleared by a drug test, had been missed during pre-departure checks. Alaska Airlines is investigating the incident.

A North Carolina judge ruled Craig Hicks, charged with fatally shooting three Muslim students in February, is eligible for the death penalty. Authorities cited a neighbor dispute over parking but are also investigating possible hate crime motives, with federal agencies conducting a parallel inquiry.

Amnesty International urges Afghan authorities to protect women's rights activists amid rising violence, citing the 2015 lynching of Farkhunda and systemic impunity for attackers. Despite threats and minimal government support, activists persist, galvanized by public displays of solidarity like women serving as pallbearers—a defiance of tradition that signals growing resistance to gender-based violence.

A New York judge authorized divorce papers to be served via Facebook private message, marking a shift toward digital methods of legal notification. Traditional in-person service remains ideal, but courts increasingly accept electronic alternatives when defendants evade contact, as online communication offers verifiable delivery and reflects modern lifestyles.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the "Hour of Power" television ministry and California's Crystal Cathedral, died at 88 after battling esophageal cancer. Known for his "possibility thinking" message and pioneering televangelism, Schuller built a megachurch empire that later collapsed amid family disputes and bankruptcy before his death.

Four workers died and 45 were injured in a major fire on Pemex’s Abkatun Permanente oil platform off Mexico’s Gulf coast. The blaze, which started in the dehydration and pumping area, was extinguished after hours of firefighting; no collapse or oil spill occurred, and the cause remains under investigation.

Kansas has enacted the first U.S. law banning dilation and evacuation abortions, a common second-trimester procedure, with exceptions only to protect the mother's life or health. Supporters hail it as groundbreaking; opponents call it dangerous and the nation’s most restrictive abortion law. Both sides anticipate legal challenges and efforts to replicate or block similar laws in other states.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized for using a racial slur on a hot mic after Saturday's loss to Wisconsin, saying it was "in jest" and not meant to disrespect Wisconsin star Frank Kaminsky. Kaminsky said he accepted Harrison’s apology and considers the matter resolved.

"Arrested Development" will return for a fifth season of 17 episodes, executive producer Brian Grazer confirmed, though Netflix declined to comment. The revival follows the show’s 2013 fourth season on Netflix after its original Fox cancellation; cast participation remains unconfirmed.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has restarted after a two-year shutdown, with beams circulating again in its 27-km ring following final tests at CERN. Operating at near light-speed, the LHC aims to recreate Big Bang conditions to probe unanswered questions in physics, including dark matter, the origin of mass, and the matter-antimatter imbalance.

An Iranian military observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of a U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf, prompting concerns that local Iranian commanders may have acted without central authority. The unsafe encounter, which occurred during nuclear talks in Switzerland, has led the U.S. to consider a formal protest, though no shots were fired and the helicopter disengaged calmly.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts, including 17 capital charges, in the Boston Marathon bombing. The trial now moves to a penalty phase where jurors will decide if he receives the death penalty, weighing aggravating factors against mitigating circumstances like his age and alleged influence by his deceased older brother.

Indian police arrested four FabIndia employees in Goa after Education Minister Smriti Irani discovered a surveillance camera overlooking a store changing room. Authorities charged the staff with voyeurism and breach of privacy, sealed the store, and summoned company officials; FabIndia expressed shock and pledged full cooperation with the investigation.

Iran plans to lift its decades-long ban on women attending men's sports events, starting with indoor games within the next year, according to Deputy Sports Minister Abdolhamid Ahmadi. The move follows international pressure, including criticism from FIFA, and comes after past brief allowances under moderate leadership were reversed.

Former Satyam chairman Ramalinga Raju and nine others received seven-year jail terms for orchestrating a $1.6 billion fraud, India's largest corporate scandal, involving inflated profits and fictitious assets. Convicted of cheating and criminal conspiracy, Raju was also fined $804,000; Satyam was later acquired by Tech Mahindra after the government ousted its board.

Elizabeth Sedway was removed from an Alaska Airlines flight in Hawaii after disclosing she had cancer and felt weak, prompting the airline to consult MedLink per policy. Though later allowed to fly home to San Jose and issued an apology, refund, and hotel reimbursement, Sedway said the incident caused her to miss chemotherapy and disrupted her family’s schedule.

Turkish singer-songwriter Kayahan, renowned for his love songs and 1991 breakthrough album "I Made a Vow," died of cancer in Istanbul at age 66. First diagnosed in 1990, his illness recurred in 2005 and 2014; he performed as recently as Valentine’s Day. Prime Minister Davutoglu mourned his passing, praising his enduring contribution to Turkish music.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the Iran nuclear deal, calling it "very bad" and urging stronger pressure instead. U.S. officials defended the agreement as a viable path to block Iran’s bomb-making capability, while Republicans and some Democrats sparred over its merits and Israel’s vocal opposition.

A suspected domestic kidnapping led to a series of connected shootings near the U.S. Census Bureau in Suitland, Maryland, and on Washington’s H Street, leaving a guard critically wounded and both a suspect and officer injured. The chase ended in a crash and shootout; the kidnapping victim was found unharmed.

Imprisoned whistleblower Chelsea Manning has joined Twitter, dictating tweets via phone to a media firm due to no internet access in prison. Serving a 35-year sentence for the largest U.S. classified leak, Manning—diagnosed with gender dysphoria and undergoing hormone therapy—is using the platform to engage with followers despite restrictions.

Rapper Nelly was arrested in Tennessee on felony drug charges after state troopers stopped his bus for missing required stickers and found methamphetamine, marijuana, drug paraphernalia, multiple firearms, and suspected drug packaging. He was booked into Putnam County Jail but later posted bond and was released.

A Delaware family fell critically ill during a stay at a U.S. Virgin Islands resort, likely due to methyl bromide pesticide exposure in their rented villa, the EPA said. The father is stable, his two sons remain in critical condition, and the mother has been released; the Justice Department has launched a criminal investigation.

Online journalists and bloggers across Asia face escalating legal persecution and deadly violence for criticizing governments or religious orthodoxy, as authoritarian regimes restrict internet freedoms and non-state actors target dissenters with impunity. From Singapore to Bangladesh, authorities use defamation laws, anti-state charges, and surveillance to silence critics, while Islamist militants in Bangladesh have murdered secular bloggers without consequence.

Nina Dobrev announced her departure from "The Vampire Diaries" after Season 6, prompting fan backlash over the show’s planned seventh season without her. Many expressed grief over the potential unresolved fate of Elena and Damon’s relationship, while producers affirmed support for Dobrev’s exit and pledged to continue the series.
ISIS stormed

NASA scientists outline a concrete path to detecting extraterrestrial life within decades, citing thousands of exoplanets—many Earth-like—and the likelihood of simple life being common. However, intelligent, communicative civilizations are probably exceedingly rare and temporally mismatched, making actual contact unlikely soon despite advances like the James Webb Space Telescope.

Carlos Colina, 32, faces murder charges after human remains identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien were found in a Cambridge duffel bag and nearby apartment building. Authorities say the two men knew each other, and Colina was previously arraigned on assault charges in an unrelated case.

Kanye West has settled a civil lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos, whom he assaulted at LAX in 2013, offering an apology and shaking hands as part of the agreement. The case, which was set for trial, was dismissed after both parties reached a confidential settlement; West had previously pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery and received probation, anger management, and community service.

President Obama’s deep political and legacy-driven investment in securing a nuclear deal with Iran has weakened U.S. negotiating leverage, resulting in a framework agreement that critics argue concedes too much—allowing Iran to retain significant nuclear infrastructure and easing sanctions prematurely. Despite Obama’s 2012 vow to demand Iran end its nuclear program entirely, the emerging deal falls far short, leaving Iran as a de facto nuclear threshold state and fueling regional fears of proliferation and instability.

The fatal shooting of unarmed black man Walter Scott by North Charleston police officer Michael Slager—captured on video—sparked national outrage and murder charges, exposing discrepancies with initial police accounts. The incident underscores a systemic lack of reliable data on police use of deadly force, despite a 1994 federal law mandating such collection, leaving critical questions about racial bias and accountability unanswered.

Five U.S. health workers exposed to Ebola in Sierra Leone have been released from monitoring in Omaha after showing no symptoms; they were part of a group linked to a colleague now in fair condition at NIH. The CDC expects all 17 monitored individuals to be cleared by Thursday, as the West African outbreak has killed over 10,000 since late 2013.

Mark Ronson and Bruno Mars' "Uptown Funk!" claims a 13th week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, becoming the longest-leading hit of the 2010s and only the 10th song in chart history to log at least 13 weeks atop the tally. Meanwhile, Natalie La Rose debuts in the top 10 with "Somebody," featuring Jeremih.

April 8 marked both "Lost" fans' numerological celebration and "Rex Manning Day" from the film *Empire Records*. The article also highlights other movie-inspired dates, including April 14 (*Titanic*), April 25 (*Miss Congeniality*), October 3 (*Mean Girls*), and October 21, 2015 (*Back to the Future Part II*).

"Grace of Monaco," starring Nicole Kidman as Grace Kelly, will premiere on Lifetime on May 25 after The Weinstein Co. bypassed a U.S. theatrical release following poor international performance and creative disputes between director Olivier Dahan and Harvey Weinstein over the final cut. The film, criticized by Kelly’s children as historically inaccurate, had been considered an Oscar contender before being pulled from awards contention and delayed multiple times.

Shibuya ward in Tokyo approved an ordinance granting same-sex couples "partnership certificates," affording limited rights like hospital visitation and joint tenancy, though not full marriage equality. The move, hailed as a symbolic step forward by LGBT advocates, may inspire other districts like Setagaya to follow, though national legal recognition remains absent.

California's historic drought, now in its fourth year, threatens national food supplies and prices, as the state produces over a third of U.S. vegetables and nearly two-thirds of fruits and nuts. Mandatory water cuts are in place, and while some produce prices spiked in 2014, economists remain uncertain about 2015 impacts due to factors like a strong dollar and low oil prices. Meanwhile, Western drought conditions also strain beef production, though California wine quality has paradoxically improved.

The University of Michigan reversed its decision to cancel a student event screening of "American Sniper" after backlash, citing commitment to free expression. Over 200 students had petitioned against the film, citing concerns over its portrayal of the Middle East, but a counter-petition and criticism led officials to reinstate the showing alongside an alternative screening of "Paddington."

Amy Schumer dominated the 2015 MTV Movie Awards with sharp comedy, while Channing Tatum twerked for Jennifer Lopez and Rebel Wilson slipped in a risqué joke. Highlights included energetic musical performances and heartfelt tributes, though some gags—like Schumer’s archery fail and dated movie references—fell flat.

A 20- to 30-foot fiberglass boat fragment, likely debris from Japan’s 2011 tsunami, washed ashore off Oregon and was towed to Newport. Biologists found yellowtail jack fish native to Japanese waters inside; deemed low ecological risk, the debris will be landfilled while the fish go to the Oregon Coast Aquarium.

One year after Boko Haram kidnapped 276 schoolgirls from Chibok, Nigeria, over 200 remain missing despite global outcry and the #BringBackOurGirls campaign. Incoming President Muhammadu Buhari pledged to crush the militants, but Boko Haram still controls parts of the northeast, and abductions continue.

Easter’s Triduum—Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and Easter Sunday—marks a profound spiritual journey from suffering through uncertainty to resurrection, reflecting universal human experiences of loss, transition, and renewal. Though rooted in Christian tradition, its themes resonate beyond religion, offering a timeless pattern of moving from darkness into light that resists commercialization.

Kenya froze 86 bank accounts linked to Al-Shabaab suspects following the Garissa University massacre that killed 147, mostly students. Authorities launched airstrikes on Al-Shabaab camps in Somalia and offered a $215,000 reward for information leading to the capture of attack organizer Mohamed Mohamud. The government faced criticism over its delayed response despite prior intelligence, as Kenyans mourned victims and demanded accountability.

Jia Jiang, a Chinese-born American entrepreneur, overcame his fear of rejection by undertaking 100 public challenges—like requesting custom Olympic-ring donuts—and documented the journey in his book *Rejection Proof*. His viral experiment transformed rejection into opportunity, leading to media appearances and speaking engagements, while promoting the idea that embracing rejection can unlock personal and professional growth.

Attorney General Eric Holder banned all Justice Department personnel from soliciting or accepting commercial sex, regardless of local laws, citing links to human trafficking. The directive follows an inspector general report revealing DEA agents attended cartel-funded sex parties overseas and highlights past misconduct by federal agents involving prostitutes. Violations will result in suspension or termination, even during off-duty or personal time.

Authorities are investigating whether the fatal shooting of Ron Lane, a gay employee at Wayne Community College in North Carolina, was a hate crime. Suspect Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, a former work-study student recently dismissed, fled to Florida after the killing and was arrested on a beach; he had a knife and facial tattoos, prompting scrutiny of possible white supremacist ties.

Amnesty International's 2015 report highlights a global rise in death sentences in 2014, with governments increasingly using capital punishment to combat terrorism and crime despite evidence it is not an effective deterrent. While executions fell overall—from 778 to 607 worldwide—troubling trends emerged in China, Pakistan, Iran, Egypt, and Nigeria, where mass trials and expanded death penalty laws reflected political or security-driven motives.

A Duke University student admitted to hanging a noose on campus and has been removed pending a conduct review; criminal investigations continue. The incident sparked protests and condemnation from students, faculty, and university leadership, who called it a "cowardly act" amid a wave of recent racist events at U.S. colleges.

Emmy-winning actor Richard Dysart, best known for playing senior partner Leland McKenzie on NBC’s “L.A. Law,” has died at age 86 after a long illness. A versatile performer with roles ranging from doctors to presidents, he appeared in every episode of the series and won an Emmy in 1992.

Easter, celebrating Christ's Resurrection, falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon following the vernal equinox, leading to varying dates and separate observances between Western and Eastern Orthodox Christians. The holiday’s symbols—eggs and the bunny—stem from medieval European customs tied to Lenten traditions and spring fertility lore, while its timing aligns with Passover due to shared lunar calculations. Pope Francis marked Easter with calls for global peace, and a recent blood moon coincided with the holiday, reflecting its astronomical roots.

Comedian Chris Rock reignited debate over racial profiling by documenting three traffic stops in seven weeks, highlighting the "driving while black" phenomenon amid ongoing tensions over police treatment of African Americans. His tweets drew both support and criticism, echoing his past comedy about avoiding police encounters—such as bringing a white friend along—as seen in a 2014 segment with Jerry Seinfeld that ended in a traffic stop.

Robert Lewis Burns Jr., original drummer for Lynyrd Skynyrd, died at 64 in a single-vehicle crash in Cartersville, Georgia. Unrestrained, he struck a mailbox and tree shortly before midnight; no other vehicles were involved. Burns, who left the band in 1975 due to tour exhaustion, was part of the group’s founding lineup but survived the 1977 plane crash that killed three members.

A photo of a cat on stairs has sparked viral debate online over whether it's ascending or descending, echoing past optical illusion controversies like #TheDress. The image, originally posted on Imgur and amplified by 9gag, has drawn varied interpretations based on the cat's motion and stair construction, with advertisers already capitalizing on the confusion.

The U.S. and P5+1 partners reached a strong nuclear framework deal with Iran, significantly curbing its program and enabling rapid detection of any covert weapons efforts. Critics’ claims—that the deal allows unchecked future enrichment, excludes key issues like missiles, or lacks multilateral backing—are factually inaccurate; the agreement imposes lasting verification measures and was negotiated collectively, not bilaterally.

Rolling Stone retracted its discredited 2014 article on a purported gang rape at the University of Virginia, but the fallout highlighted ongoing concerns about UVA’s handling of sexual assault cases—having never expelled a student for such an offense despite numerous allegations. Multiple investigations, including by the Virginia attorney general and the U.S. Department of Education, are examining the university’s policies, while survivors and advocates fear the retraction may deter victims from coming forward.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed early Wednesday outside a New York nightclub, sustaining wounds to his elbow and abdomen; two Atlanta Hawks players, Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, were arrested on obstruction and disorderly conduct charges after intervening at the scene. The suspect, who did not enter the club, remains in custody, and Copeland is in stable condition.

Twisted Sister announces its final tour, "Forty and F*ck It," marking the band's 40th anniversary and farewell. The lineup features new drummer Mike Portnoy, replacing the late A.J. Pero, with two tribute shows planned in Pero’s honor.

John Travolta dismissed HBO's critical Scientology documentary "Going Clear," calling it negative hearsay and praising his 40-year experience with the church, which he credits with helping him cope after his son's death. The actor, promoting his new film in Clearwater, Florida, said he hasn't seen the doc and doesn't plan to, asserting it reflects disgruntled former members' views, not his own.

"Furious 7" drew emotional reactions from audiences for its heartfelt tribute to the late Paul Walker, who died before filming finished. Using body doubles, CGI, and his brothers, filmmakers retired his character Brian with a poignant beach scene and a montage set to "See You Again," avoiding killing him off to honor Walker respectfully.

Season 5 of "Game of Thrones" premieres globally, advancing major storylines beyond George R.R. Martin’s books, with key character arcs converging—including Tyrion meeting Daenerys and Stannis clashing with the Night’s Watch. The season escalates toward a climax, spotlighting the Stark sisters, Cersei, and rising unrest among Westeros’ war-weary common folk.

Multiple individuals have survived extraordinary ordeals at sea, including Louis Jordan (rescued after 66 days adrift off North Carolina), Jose Salvador Alvarenga (14 months alone in the Pacific), Ron Ingraham (12 days near Hawaii), Adrian Vasquez (26 days from Panama to near the Galapagos), and Hiromitsu Shinkawa (swept out to sea by Japan’s 2011 tsunami). Each relied on ingenuity, luck, and sheer will to survive with minimal food, water, or hope of rescue.

The first six "Star Wars" films debut on digital HD Friday, featuring exclusive behind-the-scenes content, including sound designer Ben Burtt revealing the animal sources for Geonosian sounds from "Attack of the Clones." The release also introduces the franchise's first gay character.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts related to the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings, which killed three and injured hundreds. Survivors and victims’ families expressed relief and a sense of accountability, though many stressed that no verdict could fully heal their wounds or replace lost lives.

China’s former security chief Zhou Yongkang, once a top Politburo Standing Committee member, has been formally charged with bribery, abuse of power, and leaking state secrets—the highest-ranking official ever prosecuted for corruption. His trial in Tianjin marks a pivotal moment in President Xi Jinping’s anti-gr

A 21-year-old quadriplegic man with cerebral palsy was found abandoned for over four days in Philadelphia’s Cobbs Creek Park, suffering from dehydration, malnutrition, and injuries. His mother has been charged with multiple offenses, including aggravated assault and kidnapping, after allegedly leaving him there Monday before traveling to Maryland; she was arrested Sunday and faces extradition to Philadelphia.

Walmart's opposition to Arkansas' religious freedom bill—echoed by other major businesses—helped prompt GOP Gov. Asa Hutchinson to demand changes before signing, highlighting corporate influence in advancing LGBT protections. The backlash in Arkansas and Indiana reflects a broader shift in business and public opinion toward supporting gay rights, pressuring Republicans to reconcile conservative values with economic and social realities.

A lapsed Catholic recounts how Pope Francis’s compassionate tone and emphasis on inclusion—exemplified by his outreach to marginalized groups and focus on Gospel foundations—reignited her faith after years of feeling rejected by the Church. Cardinal Gerald Lacroix affirms the Pope’s approach as rooted in humility, prayer, and openness, stressing that while doctrine remains unchanged, the Church welcomes all without rejection.

Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential run makes her an unavoidable symbol of gender equality, burdening her with expectations no male candidate faces. Whether she wins or loses, her campaign will be wrongly seen as a referendum on women’s political viability, despite evidence that female candidates perform equally to men and that partisanship, not gender, dominates presidential outcomes.

Amnesty International reports a global decline in executions in 2014 but a 28% rise in death sentences, citing governments' use of capital punishment to counter terrorism or unrest. While executions fell to at least 607 worldwide (excluding China, which executes thousands secretly), mass sentencing surged in countries like Egypt and Nigeria. The U.S., Iran, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia remain among the top executioners, and most death penalty cases globally failed to meet fair trial standards.

Japanese Defense Minister Gen Nakatani told parliament that the Air Self-Defense Force has never encountered extraterrestrial UFOs, despite scrambling jets to investigate unidentified aerial objects. The response came after flamboyant lawmaker Antonio Inoki, who claims to have seen a UFO, asked about alien threats and related research.

Mark Wahlberg will star as former Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis in "Patriots' Day," a film about the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing and subsequent manhunt, produced by CBS Films. The project, which Wahlberg is also producing, draws on reporting from CBS News' "60 Minutes" and follows Fox's announcement of a competing film, "Boston Strong."

Martin O’Malley and Jim Webb, both long-shot Democratic presidential hopefuls, appeared together at an Iowa party dinner, highlighting their starkly different styles: O’Malley embraced retail politics with energetic outreach, while Webb remained reserved, more comfortable discussing veterans’ issues. Both trail far behind Hillary Clinton in polls and face uphill battles for the 2016 nomination.

Nine British citizens, including four children, were arrested in Turkey on suspicion of attempting to cross illegally into Syria. The group—three men, two women, and four minors—was detained at the Turkey-Syria border; motives remain unclear. The UK Foreign Office is seeking details from Turkish authorities.

The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted FedEx on 15 criminal counts, including conspiracy, drug trafficking, and money laundering, alleging the company knowingly shipped prescription drugs for illegal online pharmacies since at least 2004. FedEx argues it is a common carrier legally exempt from liability for contents it unknowingly transports, calling the charges legally unsound.

Kenyans mourn 147 killed in Garissa University attack, the deadliest since the 1998 U.S. Embassy bombing, as social media campaigns like #147notjustanumber share victims' stories. Al-Shabaab militants targeted Christian students, killing 142 students and five security personnel; one attacker was identified as the son of a local chief. Churches held emotional Easter services under armed guard, recalling past attacks including the 2013 Westgate Mall siege.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman documents fathers taking full advantage of Sweden’s generous 480-day parental leave policy, which includes 60 non-transferable “daddy months” and a gender-equality bonus to encourage shared caregiving. Despite the policy, only 12% of couples split leave equally, but participating fathers report deeper bonds with their children and greater appreciation for parenting’s demands. Bavman aims to photograph 60 such fathers for an upcoming exhibition and book.

President Obama reaffirmed U.S. commitment to Israel’s military edge amid criticism of the Iran nuclear deal, asserting the agreement offers a “once-in-a-lifetime” chance to curb Iran’s nuclear program through strict limits and inspections. He argued that even if Iran is untrustworthy, the deal provides crucial oversight to prevent it from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

A surge in state-level Religious Freedom Restoration Acts, like Indiana’s new law, has sparked national debate over whether such measures enable discrimination against LGBTQ+ individuals. While legal claims under these laws are rare and often involve religious minorities—not mainstream Christian groups—key cases highlight tensions between religious practice and federal regulations, from Native American eagle feather use to sacramental tea in a Brazilian church. Courts have sometimes sided with religious claimants, but victories are inconsistent, and critics argue the laws offer limited real protection.

Five Chinese feminist activists face up to five years in prison on charges of "assembling a crowd to disturb public order" after being detained ahead of International Women's Day for planning anti-sexual harassment campaigns. Their detention has sparked international condemnation and protests, with rights groups asserting their actions were lawful and aligned with China’s own gender equality policies.

Selena’s family is developing “Selena the One,” a digital embodiment using advanced hologram-like technology to walk, talk, sing, and dance as the late Tejano star. The project, led by tech firm Acrovirt LLC, aims to release new music, collaborate with artists, and tour in 2018—without replacing Selena but extending her legacy. A $500,000 Indiegogo campaign launches April 16 to support the initiative.

Former Rep. Michele Bachmann likened President Obama to Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, accusing him of steering the U.S. toward disaster with the Iran nuclear deal. Her inflammatory Facebook post drew widespread condemnation as offensive and disrespectful. Bachmann, a vocal Iran hawk, previously urged Obama to bomb Iranian nuclear sites during a 2014 White House event.

Ryan Gosling’s directorial debut "Lost River," set in a decaying yet resilient Detroit, draws inspiration from the city’s abandoned neighborhoods and ongoing urban renewal. Though divisive among critics, the film captures both the devastation and hope in post-industrial Detroit, reflecting Gosling’s deep personal connection to the city. It opens in limited U.S. and UK release on April 10.

A 19-year-old UK national, Yahya Rashid, was charged with terror offenses after being arrested at Luton Airport upon returning from Istanbul. He faces charges of preparing acts of terrorism and assisting others in committing such acts between November 1 and March 31. Rashid is set to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court.

Vince Neil’s widely panned performance of the national anthem before an Arena Football League game reignited debate over celebrity renditions of "The Star-Spangled Banner." The piece recalls iconic and infamous versions by Whitney Houston, Roseanne Barr, Jimi Hendrix, and Michael Bolton, highlighting how the anthem can elevate or embarrass its performers.

Nearly 2,000 World War I-era inscriptions by soldiers—mostly Australian, British, and American—have been discovered in an ancient underground quarry near Naours, France, used as a refuge during the war. Photographer Jeff Gusky calls the site a "treasure trove," noting the graffiti, some by men who died shortly after writing them, offers a poignant human link to the past.

The Palestinian Authority became the 123rd member of the International Criminal Court, granting the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories since June 13, 2014. Israel and the U.S., both non-members, opposed the move, while rights groups welcomed it as a step toward justice; the ICC has opened a preliminary examination that could lead to war crimes investigations involving both Israelis and Palestinians.

Anthony Ray Hinton, 58, was released from Alabama’s death row after nearly 30 years following dismissal of murder charges tied to 1985 killings, after ballistics evidence failed to link him to the crimes. Maintaining his innocence throughout, Hinton cited systemic failures involving race, poverty, and inadequate legal defense, while prosecutors declined to retry the case.

Most American taxpayers receive refunds averaging nearly $3,000, turning Tax Day into a spending spree thanks to simplified filing and free software. Despite systemic inequities—like marriage penalties and light taxation of capital gains—the immediate payoff overshadows deeper flaws in the U.S. tax system.

Jordan Spieth maintained a commanding four-shot lead after a steady third round at the 2015 Masters, despite a late double bogey. Chasers including Justin Rose (12 under), Phil Mickelson (11 under), and Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy (both 6 under) made moves but couldn't close the gap significantly.

Liana Barrientos, 39, faces criminal charges for allegedly entering into 10 marriages—eight simultaneously—as part of an immigration scam, falsely claiming her 2010 union was her first. Prosecutors say several husbands, from "red-flagged" countries, sought residency through the fraudulent marriages, with divorces occurring only after approvals; one husband was deported in 2006. Barrientos pleaded not guilty and was separately arrested for subway fare evasion; she faces up to four years if convicted, with her next court date set for May 18.

Memories Pizza in Walkerton, Indiana, sparked national controversy after its owners said they would refuse to cater same-sex weddings, citing religious beliefs under the state’s new Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The pizzeria faced boycotts, online harassment—including threats that led to a temporary closure—and a flood of negative reviews, but also received over $842,000 in donations from supporters defending their stance.

Mindy Kaling’s brother, Vijay Chokalingam, admitted to posing as Black on medical school applications to expose what he claims is unfair affirmative action advantage, sparking backlash for fraud and insensitivity. Despite receiving one acceptance, his stunt ignored systemic barriers faced by minorities and misrepresented the purpose of race-conscious admissions aimed at addressing severe underrepresentation in medicine.

Antarctica recorded a possible record high of 63.5°F (15.5°C) at Argentina’s Esperanza Base on March 24. The World Meteorological Organization has convened a panel to verify the reading, with a final determination expected by late summer or early fall.

The U.S. has abandoned its spring timeline for an Iraqi-led offensive to retake Mosul from ISIS, citing the operation’s complexity and need for further preparation. While progress has been made elsewhere—such as the recent recapture of Tikrit—officials stress that Mosul’s size, strategic importance, and entrenched ISIS presence require a more deliberate approach, with no U

Paddy Power deleted a controversial tweet comparing Newcastle's losses at Liverpool's Kop end to police killings of unarmed Black Americans, sparking backlash despite calling it a "joke." The Irish betting firm, known for publicity stunts, faced calls for accountability as Liverpool beat Newcastle 2-0 in the Premier League.

Philadelphia police charged Nyia Parler with attempted murder and other offenses after she allegedly left her quadriplegic 21-year-old son in Cobbs Creek Park for over four days before fleeing to Maryland. Parler, currently in custody in Maryland undergoing unspecified treatment, cannot be extradited until it is completed. The victim, found dehydrated and injured, is hospitalized while authorities investigate potential systemic failures in his care.

A South Korean court has charged Kim Ki-Jong with attempted murder, assaulting a foreign envoy, and business obstruction for stabbing U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert in Seoul on March 5. Kim, who opposes U.S.-South Korea military drills and has visited North Korea multiple times, must face trial within 14 days; Lippert suffered serious but non-permanent injuries.

Jill Duggar Dillard, the first daughter from "19 Kids and Counting" to marry, has given birth to her first child, a 9-pound, 10-ounce son named Israel David. The baby arrived more than a week past his due date, and Jill, a student midwife, said she remained patient, noting first-time mothers often go overdue.

"Furious 7" is on track for a $135M–$138M North American debut—the biggest since late 2013—and a potential $300M global opening, fueled by massive interest in the late Paul Walker's final film. The Universal release, playing in over 14,500 screens worldwide (excluding China, Japan, and Russia), marks the studio’s widest rollout ever and is set to claim 2015’s top opening weekend.

A Secret Service supervisor, Xavier Morales, has been placed on administrative leave and had his security clearance suspended following allegations of sexual assault by a subordinate. The incident, which occurred at a March 31 party and involved unwanted advances and physical contact, adds to a string of recent scandals plaguing the agency. Director Joe Clancy called the allegations “very disturbing,” and the case will be investigated by the Office of the Inspector General.

Hillary Clinton launches her 2016 presidential bid with strong experience and name recognition but faces challenges over authenticity, voter enthusiasm, and comparisons to Al Gore’s 2000 campaign. Her team plans a low-key rollout focused on direct voter contact to counter perceptions of inevitability and address concerns about trust, policy vision, gender bias, and potential liabilities from Bill Clinton’s involvement.

The DOJ is negotiating with Ferguson to overhaul its police department following a scathing report exposing systemic racial discrimination, excessive force, and revenue-driven policing. Recent elections brought two Black council members to power, the police chief resigned, and the city manager stepped down, signaling political change—but the extent of reform hinges on sustained community pressure and potential structural shifts, including possible regional police integration.

Etihad Airways lost a passenger’s pet cat, Felix, after its carrier was crushed during a flight from Abu Dhabi to New York’s JFK Airport on April 1. The airline, which called such incidents “extremely rare,” is investigating and aiding search efforts with third-party specialists and detection dogs, while the owners continue searching for their missing cat.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued after drifting at sea for 66 days following a storm that capsized his sailboat off South Carolina. Despite broken supplies, scarce food and water, and multiple further capsizings, he survived by catching fish with laundry and collecting rainwater, and was found in surprisingly good condition by the crew of a container ship. Coast Guard officials confirmed his account, and he was hospitalized in Norfolk, Virginia, before planning to return to his marina home.
